summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes  a square modulo p; choosing the sign of a square root y so that y\le p/2 and setting n=y-1 gives p\mid y^2-5=n^2+2n-4. The continuant recurrence expresses the relevant fraction as D_2/D_3 with D_2=pm; bounds on y (with the few small values handled separately) give m\mid(n-3)!, hence D_3=mb, while p\nmid b because otherwise p would divide 2(n-1)(n-3)!, so reduction cancels exactly m and leaves numerator p.

full_proof.text: Let \[ R_2(n)=2-\frac3{3-\frac4{4-\frac5{\ddots-\frac{n}{-4}}}}}. \] Thus the continued fraction in the statement is \(1/R_2(n)\). We shall prove that, for every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), one can choose \(n\ge3\) such that the numerator of \(R_2(n)\), in lowest terms and up to sign, is \(p\). It then follows immediately that the reduced denominator of \(1/R_2(n)\) is \(p\). We first develop the continuant identities needed to control this numerator. For a fixed integer \(n\ge3\), define integers \(D_k=D_k(n)\), for \(2\le k\le n\), backwards by \[ D_n=4,\qquad D_{n-1}=5n-4, \] and, for \(2\le k\le n-2\), \[ D_k=kD_{k+1}-(k+1)D_{k+2}. \tag{1} \] The terminal value is chosen because \[ (n-1)-\frac n{-4}=n-1+\frac n4=\frac{5n-4}{4} =\frac{D_{n-1}}{D_n}. \] Consequently, whenever the relevant denominators are nonzero, backward induction using (1) gives \[ R_k(n):=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}=\frac{D_k}{D_{k+1}} \qquad(2\le k\le n-1). \tag{2} \] Indeed, if \(R_{k+1}=D_{k+1}/D_{k+2}\), then \[ k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}} =k-(k+1)\frac{D_{k+2}}{D_{k+1}} =\frac{kD_{k+1}-(k+1)D_{k+2}}{D_{k+1}} =\frac{D_k}{D_{k+1}}. \] In particular, once nonvanishing has been established, \[ R_2(n)=\frac{D_2}{D_3}. \tag{3} \] We next evaluate \(D_2\) and obtain a useful expression for \(D_3\). Introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \((w_k)\) by \[ w_0=w_1=0,\qquad w_2=-1,\qquad w_3=0, \] and \[ w_{k+4}=(k+2)(w_{k+3}-w_{k+2})\qquad(k\ge0). \tag{4} \] A direct induction on \(k\) gives \[ k w_{k+3}-(k+1)w_{k+2}=(k+1)! . \tag{5} \] For completeness, the case \(k=0\) reads \(-w_2=1\). If (5) holds for \(k\), then by (4) \[ \begin{aligned} (k+1)w_{k+4}-(k+2)w_{k+3} &=(k+1)(k+2)(w_{k+3}-w_{k+2})-(k+2)w_{k+3}\\ &=(k+2)\bigl(k w_{k+3}-(k+1)w_{k+2}\bigr)\\ &=(k+2)(k+1)!=(k+2)!, \end{aligned} \] which is the next case. The recurrence (1), together with (4), yields the identity \[ (k-1)!D_k=2(k-2)D_3-w_kD_2 \qquad(2\le k\le n). \tag{6} \] Here and below factorials have their usual nonnegative-integer meaning. The cases \(k=2,3\) follow immediately from \(w_2=-1\) and \(w_3=0\). For the induction step, rewrite (1), for \(k\ge4\), as \[ (k-1)D_k=(k-2)D_{k-1}-D_{k-2}. \] Multiply by \((k-2)!\), apply (6) at \(k-1\) and \(k-2\), and use \[ w_k=(k-2)(w_{k-1}-w_{k-2}), \] which is (4) with shifted indices. The terms involving \(D_3\) simplify to \(2(k-2)D_3\), and those involving \(D_2\) simplify to \(-w_kD_2\), proving (6). We now calculate \(D_2\). Apply (6) with \(k=n\) and \(k=n-1\): \[ (n-1)!D_n=2(n-2)D_3-w_nD_2, \tag{7} \] \[ (n-2)!D_{n-1}=2(n-3)D_3-w_{n-1}D_2. \tag{8} \] Multiply (7) by \(n-3\), multiply (8) by \(n-2\), and subtract. The \(D_3\)-terms cancel. By (5), with its index shifted to \(n-3\), \[ (n-3)w_n-(n-2)w_{n-1}=(n-2)!. \] Using \(D_n=4\), \(D_{n-1}=5n-4\), and \((n-1)!=(n-1)(n-2)!\), the left side of the subtraction is \[ \begin{aligned} &(n-3)(n-1)!\cdot4-(n-2)(n-2)!(5n-4)\\ &=(n-2)!\bigl(4(n-3)(n-1)-(n-2)(5n-4)\bigr)\\ &=-(n-2)!(n^2+2n-4). \end{aligned} \] The right side is \(-(n-2)!D_2\). Since \((n-2)!\ne0\), cancellation gives \[ D_2=n^2+2n-4. \tag{9} \] We also need a divisibility property of \(w_n\). From (4), one checks inductively that for every \(j\ge0\), both \(w_{j+4}\) and \(w_{j+4}-w_{j+3}\) are even. The initial case is immediate, and if both quantities are even, then \[ w_{j+5}=(j+3)(w_{j+4}-w_{j+3}) \] is even, after which \(w_{j+5}-w_{j+4}\) is also even. It follows that \[ 2(n-2)\mid w_n \tag{10} \] for every \(n\ge3\) except \(n=4\). For \(n=3\), this is immediate from \(w_3=0\). For \(n\ge5\), write \[ w_n=(n-2)(w_{n-1}-w_{n-2}); \] the difference in parentheses is even by the preceding observation. The exception \(n=4\) is genuine: \(w_4=2\), which is not divisible by \(4\). We now choose \(n\) from the given prime. Let \(p\) be prime and suppose \[ p\equiv1\quad\text{or}\quad9\pmod {10}. \] Such a prime satisfies \(p\ge11\). Moreover, \(p\equiv1\) or \(4\pmod5\), so \(p\) is a nonzero square modulo \(5\). Quadratic reciprocity, together with \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), gives \[ \left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1. \] Thus there is an integer \(x\) such that \[ x^2\equiv5\pmod p. \] Replacing a residue \(x\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\) by \(p-x\) if necessary, choose a representative \(y\) satisfying \[ 0\le y\le \frac p2,\qquad y^2\equiv5\pmod p. \tag{11} \] In fact \(y\ge4\). If \(y=0,1,2,3\), then \(p\) would divide, respectively, one of \[ 5,\quad4,\quad1,\quad4, \] which is impossible because \(p\ge11\). Set \[ n=y-1. \tag{12} \] Then \[ 3\le n\le p-2, \] and, by (9), \[ D_2=n^2+2n-4=(n+1)^2-5=y^2-5. \tag{13} \] Therefore \(p\mid D_2\). Also \(D_2>0\), because \(n\ge3\). Hence there is a positive integer \(m\) such that \[ D_2=pm. \tag{14} \] Equivalently, \[ pm=y^2-5. \tag{15} \] Before using (2), we verify that no intermediate \(D_j\) vanishes. First, \(D_3\ne0\). Otherwise (7), using \(D_n=4\), would say \[ 4(n-1)!=-w_nD_2. \] Since \(p\mid D_2\), this would imply \(p\mid4(n-1)!\). As \(p\) is prime, either \(p\mid4\), impossible for \(p\ge11\), or \(p\mid(n-1)!\). In the latter case a prime divisor of \((n-1)!\) is at most \(n-1\), contradicting \(n\le p-2\). Now suppose \(D_j=0\) for some \(2\le j\le n\). Identity (6) gives \[ w_jD_2=2(j-2)D_3. \] Thus \(p\mid 2(j-2)D_3\). Since \(p\) is prime, it divides \(2\), \(j-2\), or \(D_3\). The first possibility is impossible. If \(p\mid j-2\), then \(0\le j-2\le n-20\), a contradiction. Finally, if \(p\mid D_3\), then (7), together with \(p\mid D_2\), again implies \(p\mid4(n-1)!\), which was just shown to be impossible. Hence \[ D_j\ne0\qquad(2\le j\le n). \tag{16} \] This proves that all the continued-fraction tails used in (2) are defined and that (3) holds. We next show that the cofactor \(m\) in (14) is canceled from \(D_2/D_3\). First observe that \(n\ne4\). Indeed, \(n=4\) would mean \(y=5\), and then (11) would imply \(p\mid25-5=20\), impossible for a prime \(p\ge11\). Thus (10) applies, and we may write \[ w_n=2(n-2)K \tag{17} \] for some integer \(K\). From (7), \(D_n=4\), and (17), \[ 2(n-2)D_3=4(n-1)!+2(n-2)K D_2. \] Since \[ 4(n-1)!=2(n-2)\bigl(2(n-1)(n-3)!\bigr), \] cancellation of the nonzero factor \(2(n-2)\) gives \[ D_3=2(n-1)(n-3)!+K D_2. \tag{18} \] We claim that \[ m\mid(n-3)!. \tag{19} \] This is automatic if \(m=1\), so suppose \(m>1\). We first dispose of small values of \(y\). If \(y=4\), then (15) gives \(pm=11\). Since \(p\ge11\) is prime, this forces \(p=11\) and \(m=1\), contrary to the present assumption. If \(y=5\), then \(pm=20\), so the prime \(p\ge11\) would divide \(20\), impossible. If \(y=6\), then \(pm=31\), forcing \(p=31\) and \(m=1\), again a contradiction. Therefore \[ y\ge7. \tag{20} \] By the choice \(y\le p/2\), we have \(2y\le p\). Multiplying this by the positive integer \(m\), and using (15), gives \[ 2my\le mp=y^2-50\), division by \(y\) yields \[ 2m0\), every positive integer at most \(n-3\) divides \((n-3)!\), proving (19). Choose an integer \(Q\) such that \[ (n-3)!=mQ. \tag{21} \] Substituting (14) and (21) into (18), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} D_3 &=2(n-1)mQ+Kpm\\ &=m\bigl(2(n-1)Q+Kp\bigr). \end{aligned} \] Put \[ b=2(n-1)Q+Kp. \tag{22} \] Then \(b\ne0\), because \(m>0\) and \(D_3\ne0\). Equations (3), (14), and (22) now give \[ R_2(n)=\frac{D_2}{D_3}=\frac{pm}{mb}=\frac pb. \tag{23} \] It remains to prove that no factor \(p\) is canceled in the last fraction. We show \[ \gcd(p,|b|)=1. \tag{24} \] Since \(p\) is prime, it is enough to show \(p\nmid b\). Suppose instead that \(p\mid b\). Multiplying (22) by \(m\), using (21), and reducing modulo \(p\), we obtain \[ p\mid 2(n-1)(n-3)!. \] Primality of \(p\) implies that \(p\mid2\), or \(p\mid n-1\), or \(p\mid(n-3)!\).
